review.summary: Follow-up review covers only the two supplied files at snapshot sha256:b9d3f50d…. I did not run any tests. The BLOCKER from the first review is fixed. The response header and the HTML meta both set strict-origin, so a same-origin form POST now sends the real origin as Origin instead of null. If Origin is missing, Referer is used, and it is origin-only, so the token in the query string is not exposed. A literal "null" Origin cannot be parsed and is rejected. Sec-Fetch-Site must be same-origin when present. Production and non-loopback HTTP are rejected when the code resolves its settings, so it fails closed. The prior MINOR findings are fixed or acceptably handled: (1) an invalid same-origin confirmation clears the challenge and redirects to the existing login error page; (2) the vendor name is escaped; (3) adding a masked identity is correctly kept as a separate scope proposal; (4) HTTP is rejected. Properties checked and still intact: the challenge cookie is HttpOnly, uses the __Host- prefix with path=/ on HTTPS, and is SameSite=Lax. The nonce is tied to the token, the issue time and the canonical form address. Single-value form fields, the 8 KiB body limit, the 43-character format checks, equal-length timingSafeEqual, the 300-second expiry checked against the server clock, the tenant check before the atomic consume, GET/HEAD not consuming the link, and the no-store/no-referrer redirects are all retained. CSP form-action allows only the canonical origin. I found no new BLOCKER or MAJOR. One MINOR usability defect is noted below. Possible issue, not counted as a finding: if a user ever reaches the GET page on a host other than the canonical one (e.g., www vs apex), the form posts to the canonical origin without the challenge cookie and gets a 403. This only matters if email links can use a non-canonical host. No findings here does not mean the tests or the release are certified, and Firefox verification is still pending.

findings.area: capabilityConfirmation cookie name / clearCapabilityConfirmation (single fixed challenge cookie per browser); route.ts POST failure()
findings.issue: Each browser has only one challenge cookie, so opening two magic-link previews makes them interfere with each other. Opening a second link (e.g., after the user clicks 'resend', or for another vendor) overwrites the first tab's challenge. Confirming in the stale tab then fails, and failure() clears the cookie, which also breaks the newer tab's pending confirmation.
findings.evidence: The cookie name is the constant `${secure ? "__Host-" : ""}celebratedeal_access_confirmation` with path "/" for every vendor and token. Every GET calls response.cookies.set with this name. A same-origin invalid POST runs clearCapabilityConfirmation for the same name.
findings.impact: This is a usability problem, not a security issue. A user with two magic-link emails open can end up on invalid_or_expired with both pages unusable and must request or open a link again. No token is consumed and no authentication is bypassed.
findings.recommended_fix: Optional, not blocking. Either accept and document this as a known limitation, or key the challenge per token, e.g., a cookie-name suffix derived from a short hash of the token (still under __Host- and path=/), with a small cap on how many exist. Clear only that token's cookie on failure. Or at minimum, do not clear the cookie when the submitted nonce simply doesn't match the current challenge.
findings.required_test: Browser test: open preview A, then preview B in a second tab, and confirm A. Expect A to fail without breaking B (if the fix is adopted), or document the expected behavior. Then confirm B and expect a 303 redirect to the portal.
